To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Antarctic Paleogene mollusc faunas are characterized by increasing numbers of cosmopolitan and Antarctic genera with time, and that these changes reflect the development of Antarctic glaciation.

(1) the present Antarctic fauna is well established, and was so in Middle Eocene time; (2) the present Antarctic–subantarctica molluscan fauna is a relict of the Paleogene; (3) the present Antarctic ice sheet is responsible for the absence of most present-day Antarctic–subantarctican molluscs from the region; and (4) there is no evidence that Antarctica was the source of the present-day Antarctic–Subantarctican mollusc fauna

Antarctic Paleogene mollusc faunas show: (1) a regular increase in the percentages of cosmopolitan and Antarctic genera with time, (2) that the Antarctic fauna was already established by Middle Eocene time (3) that the present major Antarctic families have remained the most abundant since the Middle Eocene, (4) that glaciation was not extensive by Late Eocene and that some shoreface molluscan genera were present in the King George Island region during Oligocene and Early Miocene

Antarctic molluscs were not cosmopolitan in the Paleogene; rather, they were a distinct fauna that became increasingly endemic as the Antarctic ice cover expanded.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Antarctic molluscan fauna was well established before the ice, but that the Antarctic glaciation is reflected by the present-day composition of the molluscan fauna.
the Antarctic molluscan fauna has been in place at least since Middle Eocene (and possibly Late Cretaceous) time, and that it has been modified by glaciation since Late Paleocene time.
Antarctica has been glaciated for most of its Paleogene and Neogene history, and that the Antarctic fauna has changed markedly in composition as a result of this.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the modern Antarctic molluscan fauna was established by the Middle Eocene, and the Antarctic ice cover has been present at least since then.
Antarctica was not a ‘lost world’ during the Paleogene; it was an active part of the global biota.
Antarctica was glaciated by Late Eocene–Early Oligocene time, and that the present Antarctic molluscan fauna is a reflection of that event.
